title: CLO International Academic Month Issue 4 (Part 2) Interactive Teaching Experience of Virtual and Physical Integration in Digital Fashion Courses
description: Interview with Ineke Siersema, professor at Amsterdam Fashion Institute, discussing the teaching experience of using CLO software in courses, the new skills required for emerging industry talents, and the successful digital transformation case of the academy's partner ATACAC! The digital future of education is within reach!
transcript:
We are so very excited to hear more about your program and how CLO has been used.  
So I'm handing it over to you.  
You can start whenever you are ready.  
Okay, I’ll start and share my screen.  
Yes, please.  
Okay, thank you for having me here.  
I'm delighted to be here and I would like to talk about my work and what our students are creating with CLO3D.  
Yes, okay, that’s the one, share it.  
All right.  
Hello everyone.  
I don’t see you, but please ask questions at the end of the Q&A session. That would be nice.  
I have a lot to tell and unfortunately can’t cover everything briefly. Sorry about that.  
Okay.  
I don’t want to show everything in this presentation, but I will try to show you a lot of what we have done.  
All right.  
My presentation is titled “From Real to Virtual and Vice Versa, Implementing 3D Digital Prototyping in a Fashion Curriculum.” It’s from real to virtual and vice versa because we live in a real world, a 3D world, and we can translate that into the digital, the virtual.  
Okay.  
All right.  
So I’m going to share a bit of what you mentioned, what I learned initially, and then I will speak about the others as well.  
What I learned is that when we talk about a 3D machine or 3D in a virtual world, many things truly exist only in the virtual world, not in the physical 3D world. So the virtual world is not physical, whereas the 3D world is physical.  
I always talk about the physical world because it is one of the very important elements in the virtual world. The virtual world is a visual world, a place where you can exchange your thoughts with others. This is very, very important.  
As was said, computer 3D modeling allows designers to think about the object itself. This enables designers to focus on decisions about objects rather than drawings.  
What I said is: we live in a 3D world, we think in 3D.  
First, I will show some earlier developments, the 3D revolution, and curriculum developments.  
I’ll take the next slide.  
Yes, this is not using 3D, but there were some applications in the 1990s where it was already possible. They started with translation simulation in 3D.  
We started a pilot in 2009. No one knew anything about it or wanted anything to do with it, but we wanted it. So we initiated a pilot for 3D virtual prototyping. Around that time, we also wanted to create a mindset because it is also a mindset. What am I looking at? Is it real? In that case, it was not real enough, but we wanted to explore the possibilities.  
Pattern construction, material training countries—what was possible?  
For Prince, it was ideal to show and place patterns. Students loved this way of working.  
It encouraged them to focus on objects and discover the new.  
Many teachers were teaching in this minor, but only two teachers initially knew about 3D. So in the beginning, it was difficult. Later, we came together and many teachers became skilled in teaching this.  
Until 2014, 3D digital was not really considered the future of fashion, but the future is now; no need to wait, just do it.  
Rethinking fashion in a sustainable and innovative way.  
Our 3D digital outcomes were not accurate enough yet. We wanted it better.  
So we needed user-friendly professional software.  
Reality in drape, look and feel, avatars, tools to enlarge, and tools to create freedom of creation.  
Because we worked on this in the design department.  
You see, students needed to create digitally all that they made in real life.  
They had the digital process combined with the physical process because we find that combination most beautiful.  
Through the combination of traditional and innovative digital software, of digital craftsmanship—the hypercraft—a new generation of designers is born.  
And that is really true. It’s a new generation. I’m older than that generation, but I love it still.  
The 3D digital revolution came to Amfi (Amsterdam Fashion Institute).  
I wanted to know why students wanted this kind of working method, what was so interesting about 3D simulation?  
So I researched the influence of digital technology, especially 3D simulation technology, on the fashion design process and the consequences for education because it was necessary.  
What did Amfi need to do to facilitate this work?  
I saw students doing it, but there were not many teachers at that moment able to understand what we were doing.  
What you see is that there is a traditional design cycle, and there is a 3D digital design cycle.  
It has a big influence on the way you think and act.  
There’s a high density of ideas from the start.  
There’s an overview of the entire plan.  
Interaction and decision-making improve.  
Unique 3D products are created.  
There is 25% more design time.  
That was what I researched.  
It’s merging together because of 3D simulation.  
We see what’s happening, and it can detect failures very well in the early stages.  
I did my master’s and an interdisciplinary project.  
We set it up with a lecturer, students, and industry partners from Felder, a lingerie company, and Jakob Kock.  
We made a comparative analysis of various 3D software.  
In 2014, CLO3D was the most user-friendly, intuitive, and future-proof software for design, production, and marketing.  
We started with that, beginning with design and later production.  
The process became more self-directed.  
An overview of the entire plan.  
Detection of failures at an early stage.  
We already knew this now.  
3D simulation and render qualities were very accurate, real, and realistic even then.  
Now it’s much more user-friendly and intuitive.  
We observed a steep learning curve, which was also important.  
We saw that with the students.  
This research led to the first live virtual fashion show.  
Students researched how virtual simulation can help extend the ways of fashion presentation and how it can make fashion design processes more sustainable.  
Because sustainability is very important.  
In this project, Amber J. Slaughter, known as one of the fabricants—you might know her—was looking for a project and said, “Come on, join us.”  
This is her collection shown in the 3D environment.  
Because we were able to use CLO3D, students loved it.  
In 2016, at the graduation show, digital collections created with CLO were presented.  
On the left is Amber J. Slaughter; she made a hologram motion capture.  
There were many experiments.  
She worked digital only; she didn’t want to produce garments in real life.  
Zylva Stelava, a digital designer and entrepreneur, adapted the principle of zero waste.  
She created a collection by cutting patterns and using all waste patterns in her collection.  
Ellie-G. Pom now works as a designer at ING.  
She created her whole collection in 3D and also made it in real life. She learned CLO in about three weeks. She was very fast. She said, “I think I’m going to do it,” and the next time I spoke to her, she already had three prototypes—digital ones.  
Tamara Koff, a 3D designer and head of design at Adidas, also had a lovely collection with nice movement.  
This was really heaven for the students to work with CLO for the first time.  
Graduates were enabled to graduate with three collections.  
This is Lula’s color palette, patterns, and leftovers. Every piece was used.  
We worked on this project together with one of the families.  
She made three different outfits, experimented with movement, and showed her transformation patterns and leftovers.  
A nice small collection, which I think is somewhere in between chaos.  
All right, moving on.  
The company that inspired me a lot was Atokac in 2019.  
They were open source, rethinking how to design, present, sell, and produce.  
This was a partner for me because I could talk with them about our developments and theirs.  
What they showed was the traditional process and the digitized process.  
Maybe you already know this, but there is a significant difference: 18 months versus one month.  
In a digitized process, there is no stock because in their process, you design the pattern, present it in 3D, render it in nice quality clothing for all products, and then sell. When you have enough orders, you produce.  
These new ways of working and business models are very important, and they were the first to come up with that.  
It was really interesting for us.  
And I think the proof of concept is: does it really work? Is it really possible to realize?  
Students want to do that too.  
Let’s compare it with denim: if they do the denim minor, they want to make real denim later on.  
They know they can do it, and they are free to challenge themselves in different ways.  
The whole collection was six outfits made for six friends, showing the products and outfits.  
He had a collage modular design experiment from Winklow, the modular tool.  
He designed digital 12-in-1 garments.  
He was very exact, precise, measured everyone, including his friends, and used a body scanner—yes, we have a body scanner.  
So he could do that professionally.  
He made 12-in-1s, then figured out fabric drape testing, which is of course very important.  
Without making a prototype, he realized it and presented it in the catalog.  
This was important for teachers to understand that it was possible, even though they didn’t grasp the process at first.  
It’s important to take people along so they understand what you are doing because it is quite abstract for those not working with it.  
Curriculum developments: these turntables are very easy and nice.  
In clothing, you can make a nice garment in a minute with these.  
I like to play around with them in my presentations.  
We have the University of Applied Science, our bigger group, the Amsterdam Fashion Institute (Amfi).  
We have existed since 1952.  
Amfi has three dimensions: fashion design, fashion business and development, and fashion branding students.  
It’s the only bachelor degree program in the Netherlands covering the entire fashion chain, with programs in Dutch and English.  
Amfi invites 350 new students every year, with some dropouts, of course.  
In total, 1,100 students study fashion at Amfi from 54 countries—an interesting international community.  
Thank you.  
We have lecturers in fashion, research, and technology. They are scientifically and artistically based.  
We have Mr. and Dr. Plugins and Core, which is data as a message of material, future means of thinking, and future ways of learning.  
How do we wear digital fashion? Now it’s pop art.  
You might not have known that it would become a hot topic, but it is digital, physical, and critical.  
Critical making is for ourselves, so that’s very important.  
We have a field lab, 3D knit, and much more.  
But I’ll continue.  
The curriculum structure: there is a lot of information—read it from year one, year two, then go to year three, four, graduation.  
The foundation year one includes some labs, which are diverse.  
Then year two and year three include industrial internships, minors, and specializations.  
I’m talking about the four-year bachelor study. The starting year has two semesters, each 20 weeks.  
A minor, specialization, and internship are one semester each.  
I focus and zoom in on what we’re doing there.  
This is year two and year three. I’ll show you some information later on about the industry internship and minor specialization.  
What I want to show is that in red, classes are included, and we want to have that in the first year as well.  
In the whole second year, we have three hours a week of club classes, and then we move to projects.  
The minor and specialization include individuals.  
I’ll show you some examples.  
3D hypercraft is very famous because that’s where we started.  
Fashion and denim production in Europe also use 3D.  
Many industry partners want to implement 3D or already do.  
Students can do a lot with that.  
In the beginning, it was not so, but now it is very good.  
The blue color indicates developing programs.  
Branding is still developing, but they are implementing 3D in their minors.  
If students have that knowledge from year two, they can apply it in their process—and they do.  
What I say is: learning by doing, not just talking about it. Just do it.  
Get behind your computer, open CLO, and create.  
There is a lot of information and magic material CLO already provides.  
You can go to their YouTube channel, and you can always Google tutorials like “how to insert a zipper.”  
You get many hits.  
But this is naturally through doing.  
Here you see a sketch and a 12-in-CLO project, a small project—learning by doing.  
All students map that process each semester, from start to end product.  
It’s to communicate and reflect on their learning process.  
They show tools, techniques, working methods, design experiments, etc.  
That’s important.  
This is an eyelet created with straps in a hoodie that they also had to create and reflect on.  
They also reflect on whether they like it or not.  
What’s the bigger picture? What’s happening?  
Finding articles about 3D developments.  
This is just a lookbook from a student at Amfi.  
She shows a silhouette, her first design.  
She made really interesting digital sculptures with bodies.  
Later, she designed her outfit on them.  
With all kinds of experiments, she was able to create it digitally.  
It was a complete digital graduation project.  
What we see with the 3D revolution and implementation is that there is a new vocabulary: the 3D model, that kind of image, the model, which is really important.  
We need to learn how to place them, how to blend them.  
That is what we already know, but we had to do it and share findings because we came across many different systems.  
We need to share and talk about it, including internet launching, closing, instruction videos, YouTube, and don’t forget the manuals—they’re great.  
There is a new vocabulary like texturing. It’s not only about buying fabric; it’s about making a texture map, a normal map, a displacement map.  
It’s a whole new way of working.  
Students don’t understand it immediately; you have to repeat it.  
Then when they create and show it, the steep learning curve becomes clear.  
We can personalize our digital fabric and do whatever we want.  
Let’s see if we need it only for design or also for production.  
In a digital world for production, you have the possibility to source and understand.  
What I really love is the schematic render.  
Many people don’t know what that is.  
That is vocabulary we need to learn. What is a mesh? What is schematic render?  
You already saw an easy one: just the top of a trouser created for bottoms, with topstitches.  
Why make a flat drawing when you already have a 3D product?  
That is what students research too.  
I’m so glad CLO came up with this schematic render.  
In year two, one of the assignments at the end of the first period is to create a small collection.  
They have to make drawings like this one.  
Then they have to realize it with pattern making, sewing classes, fabric classes, etc.  
Then they recreate it digitally, making a digital twin.  
This is a very good learning part of the process.  
We collaborate with industry partners like H&M, Burley, North Face, and more, which is very motivating for students.  
What is the bigger picture?  
Going into the real world, because in the end, it’s a bubble, and we have to get out and see what’s happening.  
Matthias of Publika set up skills overview for On Feed, especially preparing for internships.  
He said the basics are CLO 3D and presentation, garment construction, basic pattern and assembly.  
That is important.  
In the first two years, our direction is on how to design from concept and learn about materials.  
Industry production-focused tasks are in the second year, second semester.  
Internships also involve patterns.  
These are all company names that love to have our students as interns.  
Our students have a lot of skills and knowledge about 3D, which has been a topic for a long time, so it is well developed.  
Students and graduates work at companies like H&M, One, or on Vivian Westwood.  
Year three and four is a flexible program.  
There is also an innovation program called the Vision Studio.  
Students work with industry partners to design the future.  
This is the reality school where the 3D dimensions work together: branders, managers, designers—sometimes mostly designers.  
There are research questions from industry partners who have not started with 3D yet.  
We introduce 3D to them and see what kind of product they have.  
Students experiment with this, including fashion business and development students and branding students.  
They define their new role as a 3D fashion zone and a 3D digital fashion brand.  
This development is very important for companies and students.  
In year three and four, it’s a flexible program.  
In 2020, there was the minor Hypercraft and a collection made by Laura Slings.  
She created a fashion picture collection.  
We developed an independent and experimental cultural collection.  
She wanted luxury brand storytelling with a critical message called “Be Careful What You Wish For,” criticizing social obstruction by the rich.  
At the end, she looks very happy in her smooth, simple dress.  
Whatever she did, she had very good research and created this from start to end, including assets on the garment and the nice lace she made.  
It was a very interesting project.  
Another more technical project developed new design methods for upcycling, smart and sustainable research.  
The technical goal was to explore if CLO3D can be used as a tool to design from existing materials.  
It was a fashion collection for urban beach commerce.  
She developed a technique to place special fabric diversity and how it fits and works in presentation.  
Here she showed different pattern pieces and some extended fuse.  
In the end, she had beautiful renders created in CLO, and all these trims she made herself.  
She said, “What I like is that I can still make changes to my design before cutting into the material, so I can evaluate whether this material is suitable or not.”  
Also, making an inlay like this is clearer and easier than I imagined in real life, which is very interesting.  
When talking about communication, vocabulary and online tools for production are also important components for digital fashion or for real production using CLO.  
Students are experimenting with CLO.  
For production, it is clear how we can communicate, and CLO helps companies do that.  
It’s really interesting.  
Everything is in nice renderings with tech packs and bomber materials.  
But if you want to communicate digital fashion, how do you do that?  
You need parameters for fabrics, such as what kind of matching, extra details, and texturing are used.  
Of course, also how the garment is connected and assembled, and some extended fuse.  
So we think not only about production in real life but also production from a digital environment.  
The fashion industry needs new people with digital craftsmanship, along with traditional skills, which is a very interesting idea.  
I think it’s a really important tool to navigate.  
It does take some data from companies that still exist in the world.  
But I think it’s very interesting to work with a lot of data from a top-level perspective.  
If this is something you want to use and you don’t want to spend time worrying about whether it’s a game or not, it can be amazing.  
There’s so much more in these kinds of resources.  
If you could put it in a bag, how would you choose it?  
Because it’s a very traditional way of thinking.  
Digital marketing is very interesting.  
There are other questions I can answer, but I’ll move on now.  
Fitting now on the hooky avatar, knowing about patterns, assembly, and material texturing is very important.  
You want realistic drape, look, and feel.  
Then automated methods—know about those.  
I showed some automated methods earlier.  
Creating pleats is so much fun and very serious in CLO3D.  
Students take that opportunity and apply it in their collections.  
Designers now show many more pleats in collections than before because it’s optimized and easy to create digitally.  
For example, puffers—there is a lot of variation in puffer jackets because that is easy to create closure here.  
This was a student who was very precise.  
Details are important, also in digital garments.  
Digital fashion details tell a story about the garments and give character, which is important.  
Moving on to more of our changemakers and skill sets: critical thinking, digital literacy and craftsmanship, software flexibility, conscious design, decision-making, respect for craft, creating value not only for own products—these are important skills for students and professionals in this field.  
As you saw in the first projects of Amber J. Slaughter, go visit the fabricant, the digital fashion house.  
They waste nothing but data, igniting a fashion revolution through co-creation with the status quo.  
They are a community wanting to learn from each other, give feedback, co-create experiences, and enjoy.  
It’s a marketplace community wanting to share knowledge and income.  
You create an NFT (non-fungible token), for instance.  
They do it together, tell people how to do it, mint it using blockchain, and then it becomes a shared creation.  
It’s very interesting and nice.  
They make clothes that are always digital and metaphysical—that principle they keep.  
Augmented reality will come back later.  
We also saw the work of Zylva Stelava.  
She shoots out digital samples to reduce weight, reuse waste, and promote clean circularity.  
She makes beautiful renders of special people, not average.  
She reuses everything that blouses and jackets have, re-assembling that to create her own style.  
She does everything 3D using CLO, of course.  
Students create their own projects.  
These are graduate projects.  
Everyone can create their own project in the last half-year of the study.  
Some focus on digital fashion care labels or digital waste.  
Can we replace a technical drawing?  
The answer, as we know now, is yes—CLO came up with a solution.  
This was a beautiful presentation.  
This is a session with management students.  
One wrote a thesis about how luxury brands prepare for metaverses.  
We are at the beginning of shaping new digital worlds.  
She wants to do it for Web 3.0 or Web 4.0, where touch and feel will be there.  
She made outfits that people can wear in that metaverse, which is very interesting.  
It’s a beautiful, technical, very well-created digital fashion capsule collection helping a smooth transition from offline to online.  
Your virtual twin—this is a chair and a garment in itself, facilitating the transition from offline to online.  
Also created by Lily Shillings.  
We have graduates who are entrepreneurs, finding niches and pushing 3D innovation forward.  
For lingerie, the development of soft tissue avatars is important for fit.  
Rosa Kramer set up this Hyperbirth Studio; she is a graduate.  
Now she has six staff members; she started two years ago.  
Moving on, we see Sarah Meyer, whom you saw in the second video.  
She first worked in the fashion industry and now is a vegan virtual artist.  
She did face filters on Pinkradia in 2015.  
It’s amazing what she creates.  
I have some links here, but mostly with CLO, I saw “Calling All Creators: Get the Chance to Make Your 3D Garments into AR Filters” at CLO Connects.  
If you want to know more about that, it’s interesting.  
She has a good website where you can try out the face filters she made.  
Well, again, from real to virtual, vice versa.  
I like to end with this joyful movie he created.  
He used wasted inflatables and reused them.  
The process is experimental and technical, with a personal signature.  
All done.  
The garments and assets were designed and created in CLO Review and executed in real life by the designer.  
He graduated last year and won the prize for best of all universities in the Netherlands.  
It’s great.  
You see him struggling, finding this flamingo, how to add it into a pattern, what is needed, what other materials are needed.  
It’s really interesting to do that in CLO because it works and immediately gives feedback in your 3D simulation.  
Okay, next is the video. Maybe you have sound; I hope so. Otherwise, just enjoy.  
Okay.  
Nice.  
Good, awesome.  
Thank you.  
It was short but very intense.  
Nice.  
Yes.  
All the materials he made are incredible, with many prints.  
Well, I hope you understood some of my talk and liked it.  
Thanks for listening.

chunks.title: CLO International Academic Month Issue 4 (Part 2) Interactive Teaching Experience of Virtual and Physical Integration in Digital Fashion Courses
chunks.content: # Interactive Teaching Experience of Virtual and Physical Integration in Digital Fashion Courses This document details the implementation of CLO3D and 3D digital prototyping in fashion education, focusing on curriculum development, student projects, industry collaboration, and the blending of traditional and digital craftsmanship. It covers technical workflows, software evaluation, pedagogy, and emerging digital fashion trends including sustainability, virtual presentations, and digital avatars. --- ## From Real to Virtual: Implementing 3D Digital Prototyping in Fashion Curriculum This section introduces the conceptual framework of translating physical 3D fashion design into digital 3D environments using CLO3D, highlighting the distinction between physical reality and virtual visualization. - The physical world is inherently 3D and tangible, while the virtual world is a visual, interactive space for idea exchange. - 3D computer modeling enables designers to focus on the object itself rather than 2D drawings. - The fashion curriculum integrates both physical and digital processes to enhance creativity and craftsmanship. - The "3D digital revolution" began with early 3D applications in the 1990s and pilot projects at Amsterdam Fashion Institute (Amfi) starting in 2009. - Initial challenges included skepticism and limited teacher expertise, but adoption grew alongside software improvements. - CLO3D emerged by 2014 as the most user-friendly and future-proof 3D fashion software, supporting design, production, and marketing workflows. - The digital design cycle differs from traditional design by enabling high idea density, better overview, improved interaction, early failure detection, and unique 3D product creation. - Students benefit from merging traditional and digital craftsmanship, forming a new generation of designers skilled in both realms. --- ## Early 3D Projects and Industry Collaboration This section discusses early student projects, industry partnerships, and the growing role of 3D virtual prototyping in sustainable fashion design and presentation. - A master's interdisciplinary project compared various 3D software; CLO3D was preferred for its intuitive interface and accurate simulation. - The first live virtual fashion show demonstrated the potential of 3D simulation to extend fashion presentation and improve sustainability. - Notable student projects include: - Amber J. Slaughter's fully digital collection with hologram motion capture, emphasizing zero physical production. - Zylva Stelava's zero-waste collection reusing all pattern scraps. - Ellie-G. Pom’s rapid mastery of CLO3D, producing both digital and physical prototypes. - Tamara Koff’s 3D-designed Adidas collection with realistic garment movement. - Graduates created collections emphasizing sustainable design practices, such as Lula’s project using all leftover fabric and transformation patterns. - Industry inspiration came from companies like Atokac, which demonstrated digitized fashion workflows reducing product lead times from 18 months to one month by producing only after sales. - Students experimented with modular design tools, body scanning for precise fit, and fabric drape simulation to replace physical prototyping. - Educators emphasized the importance of guiding teachers and students through abstract digital workflows to foster understanding and adoption. --- ## Curriculum Structure and Pedagogy at Amsterdam Fashion Institute (Amfi) This section outlines the structure of Amfi’s fashion program, focusing on the integration of 3D digital skills throughout the bachelor’s degree.

chunks.content: - Industry inspiration came from companies like Atokac, which demonstrated digitized fashion workflows reducing product lead times from 18 months to one month by producing only after sales. - Students experimented with modular design tools, body scanning for precise fit, and fabric drape simulation to replace physical prototyping. - Educators emphasized the importance of guiding teachers and students through abstract digital workflows to foster understanding and adoption. --- ## Curriculum Structure and Pedagogy at Amsterdam Fashion Institute (Amfi) This section outlines the structure of Amfi’s fashion program, focusing on the integration of 3D digital skills throughout the bachelor’s degree. - Amfi offers a four-year bachelor program covering fashion design, business, development, and branding, with an international student body of 1,100 from 54 countries. - Curriculum includes foundational labs in year one; internships, minors, and specializations in years two and three; and flexible innovation programs in years three and four. - 3D hypercraft is a flagship minor emphasizing digital craftsmanship and industry-relevant skills. - Students engage in hands-on projects using CLO3D, learning pattern making, sewing, fabric knowledge, and digital twin creation. - The learning approach is “learning by doing,” supported by abundant online resources, YouTube tutorials, and CLO3D’s own materials. - Students document and reflect on their design processes each semester, including tool usage, techniques, and personal evaluations. - Industry collaborations with companies such as H&M, Burley, North Face, and others provide real-world relevance and internship opportunities. - Advanced years incorporate interdisciplinary collaboration with business and branding students, fostering the development of new 3D fashion roles and digital brand identities. - The Vision Studio innovation program partners students with industry to address emerging 3D fashion challenges. --- ## Technical Vocabulary and Digital Fashion Skills This section elaborates on the new terminology, technical skills, and digital fashion concepts students must master. - Key vocabulary includes 3D model, texture map, normal map, displacement map, schematic render, and mesh. - Schematic renderings provide simplified technical views of garments, useful for production communication. - Students learn to create pleats, closures, and detailed digital garment elements, enhancing realism and storytelling. - Digital fabric customization allows for personalized textures and material behaviors, crucial for both design and production. - CLO3D supports tech packs, detailed trim specification, and assembly instructions digitally, streamlining communication with manufacturers. - Automated pattern construction and fitting tools improve design efficiency and accuracy. - Understanding avatars, body scanning, and soft tissue simulation is essential for fit and sizing accuracy, especially in lingerie. - Students develop critical thinking, digital literacy, software flexibility, conscious design, and respect for craftsmanship. - Digital fashion extends beyond design to marketing, including NFTs, blockchain-based co-creation, and augmented reality filters. --- ## Notable Digital Fashion Projects and Graduates This section highlights exemplary student and graduate projects that showcase the integration of digital and physical fashion design. - Amber J. Slaughter’s digital fashion house emphasizes zero waste through data-only garment creation and community co-creation via NFTs and blockchain. - Zylva Stelava promotes circularity by reusing all garment waste digitally before physical production.
